analysis.one_liner: Raised federal tobacco taxes sharply and used a slice of the money to help tobacco farmers switch to other crops.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the federal cigarette tax from 24 cents to $1.24 a pack, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 22, 1995 and never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised federal excise taxes on every tobacco product — most dramatically cigarettes, from $12 to $62 per thousand, which works out to a jump from about 24 cents to $1.24 per pack. It also taxed existing warehouse inventory to stop wholesalers from stockpiling before the increase, and closed a gap that let roll-your-own cigarette tobacco go untaxed. Three percent of the new revenue would have gone into a trust fund to pay tobacco farmers to switch to other crops and to help tobacco-dependent towns diversify.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, chiefly through public health: cigarette prices that rise by roughly a dollar a pack would push many smokers to quit and make it harder for teenagers to start, since excise taxes are passed straight into retail prices. Smokers who quit save money and live longer. Tobacco farmers who want out of the business would gain too — the trust fund could buy up their government tobacco allotments, pay for conversion to other crops, and fund grants and loans to tobacco-dependent communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, especially teens priced out of smoking

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal cigarette tax from $12 to $62 per thousand — from about 24 cents to $1.24 per pack — and raises taxes on cigars, snuff, chewing and pipe tobacco, cigarette papers, and tubes by similar multiples, effective January 1, 1996.
Higher prices are the main reason the bill is titled a consumption reduction act: excise taxes are passed through to retail prices, and paying more per pack is what leads smokers to cut back or quit.

Creates a Tobacco Conversion Trust Fund seeded with 3 percent of the net new revenue, which the Agriculture Department could spend on helping farmers convert from tobacco, buying up and retiring tobacco allotments from farmers who choose to quit, and funding grants and loans so tobacco towns can build other industries.

Imposes a one-time tax on warehouse floor stocks held on January 1, 1996 (retail shelves excepted) so distributors cannot stockpile cigarettes at the old tax rate, and taxes product sitting in foreign trade zones the same way — closing the obvious avoidance routes.
For the first time taxes roll-your-own tobacco, at $1.86 per pound, which previously escaped tobacco excise tax entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, who would pay roughly a dollar more per pack and proportionally more on other tobacco products — a cost that falls hardest on lower-income smokers who keep smoking, since tobacco taxes are regressive. Tobacco manufacturers, wholesalers (who owe tax on inventory held on January 1, 1996), and tobacco farmers, whose leaf market would shrink as smoking declines, though the trust fund partially compensates the farmers.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: the roughly $1-per-pack increase costs a pack-a-day smoker about $365 a year, and because smoking is concentrated among lower-income people, those least able to pay would bear most of it.

The farmer compensation is thin relative to the disruption: only 3 percent of the new revenue goes to the trust fund, while a tax this size would shrink cigarette sales and the demand for American-grown leaf far more broadly across tobacco-growing communities.
Very large excise increases create an incentive for smuggling and black-market cigarettes, which would erode both the revenue and the public health effect if enforcement lagged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong — a fivefold cigarette tax increase is one of the most reliable tools for cutting smoking, particularly among teenagers, and the bill quietly closes the stockpiling and roll-your-own loopholes that usually blunt such increases. The honest costs are real: the tax hits low-income smokers hardest, and 3 percent of revenue is a modest cushion for farming communities facing a structural decline. On balance this was a serious, well-drafted public health bill whose main design flaw was underfunding the transition for the people on the supply side.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from March 1995 until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997; nobody ever brought it up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Bradley introduced the bill on March 22, 1995, joined by one cosponsor, Senator Frank Lautenberg, and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day — the committee that handles all tax legislation.
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed. The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and wholesalers, who kept the existing low federal tax rates on every product, and smokers who continued buying at pre-1995 prices. Tobacco farmers got no conversion aid either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies kept the old low tax

for.name: Bill Bradley
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 22, 1995 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers, wholesalers, and growers who would bear the new taxes
against.what_they_did: Opposed tobacco excise tax increases during this era and had long-standing influence over the Finance Committee's tobacco tax agenda

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; both sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-run Senate never moved the bill.

industries.note: The cigarette tax would rise from $12 to $62 per thousand (about 24 cents to $1.24 per pack), with similar multiples on cigars, snuff, and other products, plus a one-time tax on their warehouse inventory and a new tax on roll-your-own tobacco that was previously untaxed. Their interest ran squarely against the bill, since higher prices cut sales.

A tax this size would shrink demand for American-grown leaf, but the bill was built to protect them: the Tobacco Conversion Trust Fund would buy up allotments from farmers who want out, pay for crop conversion, and fund diversification in tobacco towns. The bill treats growers as people to be transitioned, not targeted.

Wholesalers holding untaxed inventory on January 1, 1996 would owe a one-time floor stocks tax of roughly 80 percent of the new rates, and product entering from foreign trade zones would be taxed the same way. Their interest was in avoiding the tax, which would have undercut the bill's revenue and health effects.
